Venetian to Pay $7.2M Fine Over Illegal Bookmaker Ties

Published August 23, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Nevada Gaming Commission voted 3-0 on August 20 to approve a $7.2 million fine and settlement against the Venetian Resort Las Vegas, closing out a case built around the property's dealings with convicted illegal bookmaker Mathew Bowyer. It's the fourth Las Vegas Strip casino fined over ties to Bowyer, bringing the combined total across all four properties to roughly $34 million.

What the Venetian was accused of

According to the Nevada Gaming Control Board's complaint, a Venetian casino host knew as early as 2019 or early 2020 that Bowyer was operating an illegal bookmaking business, but the resort failed to report that knowledge as its anti-money-laundering program required. Over roughly 30 visits between 2019 and 2021, Bowyer deposited about $22.3 million and lost at least $3.6 million gambling at the property. Regulators found the casino failed to properly verify the source of Bowyer's funds, failed to investigate his activity, and didn't ban him from the property until March 2024 — years after his bookmaking operation had become known internally.

The violations occurred while the Venetian was owned by Las Vegas Sands Corp.; Apollo Global Management acquired the property in February 2022 and, as current owner, is the party that agreed to the settlement and enhanced compliance measures now.

A pattern across the Strip

The Venetian is the fourth Las Vegas casino fined over its dealings with Bowyer, joining MGM, Caesars, and Resorts World in settlements tied to the same illegal bookmaking operation. Nevada revised its anti-money-laundering regulations in April 2026 in the wake of these cases. Commissioner Brian Krolicki was blunt about the pattern during the vote, saying the situation "infuriates" and "embarrasses" the state.

Why it matters for players

Cases like this are a reminder that AML compliance obligations sit underneath the player-facing side of a casino, whether the games are on the floor or in a legal online product — operators are required to know their customers and flag suspicious financial activity, not just take deposits. For regulated online casino and sportsbook operators specifically, the broader point stands too: robust source-of-funds and know-your-customer checks exist to prevent exactly this kind of years-long blind eye, and enforcement actions like this one are part of how state regulators keep pressure on operators to actually run those programs rather than treat them as paperwork.
